newsitem.title: GERMANY: OPINION-Nerves on the bond markets?
newsitem.headline: OPINION-Nerves on the bond markets?

text.p: By Manfred Lindermayer, Head of Research at Hypobank

MUNICH, Germany, April 2 - As at the start of December, the trend in falling interest rates, until then intact, was again interrupted at the end of the first quarter in 1997 by a sharp countermovement of over 50 basis points. A direct impact from the bond market environment could not be pinned down immediately for either of the corrections. On the other hand, arguments for a clear gain in bond prices could once again only be derived from the still favourable availability of liquid funds. Here too, we assume that foreign investors in German bonds will not increase their current levels of investment.

Above all, it is becoming apparent that economic and monetary data no longer have a decisive supporting impact. It is indeed true that unfavourable inflation data at the start of the year as well as surprisingly strong economic data may have exaggerated the probable trend for the coming months. Nevertheless, if our forecasts for the fundamental economic conditions in 1997 are confirmed, our estimates regard an initial 6 percent for 10-year bonds as a fair evaluation of the market. The rate will shift upwards to 6.20 percent in the second half of the year. At the same time we assume that following the end of the interest rate cut cycle introduced in September 1992, the Bundesbank will not take any steps that the markets could interpret as anticyclical countermeasures.

The uncertainty in the short term undoubtedly originates in the first policy increase agreed by the FED since February 1995. The, as expected, moderate rise in the target rate of 25 basis points on March 25th followed a sequence of surprisingly strong economic data or growth indicators. They served equally as confirmation for the preceding preventative step and as occasion for fears of a series of repeated increases similar to the one seen in 1994. In our opinion, this assessment is unfounded but we do not rule out another increase in the Fed Funds of a further 25 basis points at the next FOMC meeting on May 20th.

Consequently the mood on the US bond market remains nervous and prone to further price set-backs. Even more so since the 30-year US Treasuries have again crossed the important 7 percent level for the first time since September 96. The recently frequently quoted "Emancipation" of the German bond market from developments in the US markets will reach its limits if the spread (10-year bonds to T Notes) increases by more than 100 basis points. The fact that the growth dynamic of the two economies, which are now extremely divergent, will become more alike later in the year strengthens this.

Up to now rates in German capital markets have shown themselves to be little influenced by the intensified EMU debate in the media. The spreads to the former "High-Yielders" have recently expanded as expected, but only comparatively little, without recognisable drama. The estimated yield curve derived from the fundamental actual data in our assessment model of the German bond market is almost the same as that actually shown by the market.

If one plausibly interprets the striking differences in the past two years as an indication of existing risk premiums, they have currently almost completely melted away. Looking at this from the opposite viewpoint, we conclude from this that the discussion surrounding the changing EMU probability scenarios has little effect on current bond prices.
This agrees with our assumption that the exaggerated controversy about room for flexibility in the interpretation of the deficit criteria will not in the end cause a re-evaluation.

On balance we are sticking by our assessment that in the short term it is not possible to forecast a clear trend in the German bond market. The evaluation of our underlying scenario assumptions speaks for a fundamentally justified shift of the yield level for the REX-10 to approximately 6 percent initially.

On the other hand the free cash reserves allow ever longer recovery periods, which means that the course up to the middle of the year will continue to move sidewards and will remain extremely volatile. In connection with this, we expect a steady interest rate rise to establish itself by the end of the year, heading up into the region of 6.20/6.40 percent for 10-year bonds. In the money market, if Bundesbank policy remains unchanged, we expect only a marginal rise for three-month money to about 3.40 percent.
